title: To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma
author: James Guild
text:
A train arrives at Semut station in Surabaya, Indonesia.
Credit: Flickr/Peter Velthoen
Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.[...]
